Several open-source CLIs fit this description. I didn't check their licenses or current maintenance status, so verify those before relying on any of them.

- **leakguard** is a Rust crate that redacts secrets & PII from stdin (or files) and writes to stdout. It covers emails, credit cards, IPs, JWTs, API keys, and more, and offers a --check mode that exits non-zero when sensitive data is found.
- **local-redact** is a Python package and CLI that handles email addresses, phone numbers, IBANs, card numbers... IP addresses and API keys. Its README describes stdin-to-stdout use and a JSON report, and it can skip types such as IP_ADDRESS.
- **hexredact** targets log files and offers consistent tokens, so the same value always gets the same token, which keeps logs traceable. It can read from a pipe, and UI output goes to stderr, so stdout carries only the redacted text.
- **cleansh** is a Rust tool that processes input from stdin or a specified file, redacting sensitive information such as emails, IP addresses, various tokens. It also handles both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.
- **rog7/redact** is a simple Python option: it hides emails, API keys, and tokens in a log before you share it. It prints the cleaned log to stdout, and the original file is not changed.

If you need stdin support and IP redaction, leakguard, local-redact, and cleansh look the closest from these results. The snippets don't confirm which one best suits your workflow.

**leakguard 1.0.0** (released 2026-10-06) is a Rust library and CLI that finds and removes secrets and personal data from text and logs. It has no dependencies.

- **License:** Dual-licensed under MIT or Apache-2.0, at your option.
- **Repository:** https://github.com/ptukovar/leakguard
- **Install:**
  - Library: add `leakguard = "1.0.0"` to `Cargo.toml`.
  - CLI: `cargo install leakguard`

**Usage (stdin/stdout)**

```sh
# Read from stdin, write redacted output to stdout
tail -f app.log | leakguard

# Redact from a file, keeping the last 4 characters
leakguard --mask partial --keep 4 access.log > clean.log

# Redact stdin with '#' masking, limited to emails and IPv4
leakguard --only email,ipv4 --mask char --char '#' < input.txt
```

**Detects by default**

- Email addresses, credit card numbers (Luhn-checked), IPv4 and IPv6 addresses
- JWTs, US SSNs, MAC addresses, IBANs (mod-97 checked)
- URLs with embedded credentials, PEM private keys
- API tokens: AWS, GitHub, Slack, Stripe, Google, OpenAI, Azure connection strings, Telegram, Discord

Two detectors are opt-in because they produce more false positives: phone numbers and generic high-entropy secrets.

**Key flags**

- Masking: `--mask` (partial, template, char), `--keep`, `--template`, `--char`
- Selection: `--only`, `--without`, `--ignore`, `--redact-word`, `--redact-literal`
- Output: `--stats`, `--json`, `--show-values`, `--list-kinds`
- CI checks: `--check` (exits 1 if a match is found), `--verbose`

**Exit codes:** 0 for success (including no findings under `--check`), 1 when `--check` finds a match, and 2 for usage or I/O errors.

The project describes itself as best-effort redaction, not a complete or cryptographically secure solution.

content.content:
**Latest version:** 0.1.11, released 2025-12-20. The page describes it as "Sanitize your terminal output. One tool. One purpose."

**License:** The CLI and core library are dual-licensed under MIT OR Apache-2.0, and the page says the PolyForm license no longer applies to v0.1.9 and later. Team features such as `cleansh profiles sync` are inactive stubs in the open-source CLI.

**Repository:** https://github.com/KarmaYama/cleansh-workspace

**Install:**
- From crates.io: `cargo install cleansh`
- Prebuilt binaries are available from GitHub Releases.

**Usage examples (stdin/stdout):**
- Pipe a string in: `echo "My email is test@example.com" | cleansh sanitize`
- Sanitize container logs: `docker logs my-container | cleansh sanitize`
- Sanitize a file with the entropy engine: `cat unknown_logs.txt | cleansh sanitize --engine entropy`
- Fail a CI build if secrets are found: `cat build.log | cleansh scan --fail-over-threshold 0`

**What it detects:**
- Email addresses
- IPv4 and IPv6 addresses
- JWTs
- GitHub PATs and Stripe keys
- AWS, GCP, and Azure cloud keys
- SSH keys and generic hex/tokens
- Credit card numbers, US SSNs, UK NINOs, and South African IDs
- Paths, such as replacing `/home/user` with `~/`
- Other secrets with no known format, via the opt-in entropy engine (`--engine entropy`)

**Flags shown on the page:**
- `--engine entropy`: enables the entropy engine
- `--fail-over-threshold`: sets the threshold for `scan` (used with `0` for CI failure)
- `-c`: copies output to the clipboard
- `-d`: shows a diff view
- `--config`: loads custom YAML regex rules
- `--enable` / `--disable`: turns named rules on or off

The page does not provide a full flag reference. The project's COMMANDS.md handbook is linked for that.

content.text:
I'd recommend **leakguard**. It's a small Rust command-line tool, licensed MIT/Apache-2.0, that reads from stdin and writes the redacted text to stdout. It runs entirely on your machine with built-in detectors, so you don't write any regexes.

**How I checked:** pickfit's list of tested tools had nothing for this, so I found these through a web search and read their crates.io/docs.rs pages. I haven't installed or tested either tool, and both are new projects with few users. Treat them as a first pass and still skim the output before you paste it.

## Main pick: leakguard (v1.0.0, released 2026-10-06)

**Detects by default:** emails, IPv4 and IPv6 addresses, JWTs, URLs with embedded credentials, PEM private keys, and API tokens from AWS, GitHub, Slack, Stripe, Google, OpenAI, Azure connection strings, Telegram and Discord. It also catches credit cards (Luhn-checked), IBANs, US SSNs and MAC addresses.

**Off by default (more false positives):** generic high-entropy secrets and phone numbers. Server logs often hold custom or internal tokens that match no known format, so you probably want the high-entropy detector on.

### Install
I'm assuming you don't have a Rust toolchain yet. If you do, skip to step 2.
```sh
# 1. Rust toolchain (from your distro or rustup; rustup pipes a script into sh, so read it first)
sudo apt install cargo        # Debian/Ubuntu; or: sudo dnf install cargo
# 2. Install leakguard into ~/.cargo/bin
cargo install leakguard
# make sure ~/.cargo/bin is on your PATH
```

### First run
```sh
# See which detectors exist and what they're called (including the opt-in entropy one)
leakguard --list-kinds

# Quick test
printf 'user bob@example.com from 203.0.113.7 key=ghp_abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789\n' | leakguard

# Real use: scrub a log into a clean file, then paste that
leakguard server.log > clean.log
# or straight from a pipe
journalctl -u myapp --since "1 hour ago" | leakguard > clean.log

# See what it caught (counts per type)
leakguard --stats server.log > clean.log
```
Other useful flags:
- `--check` exits with code 1 if anything sensitive is found, which works as a "safe to paste?" gate.
- `--redact-literal` / `--redact-word` add your own hostnames or customer names without writing regexes.
- `--mask partial --keep 4` keeps the last 4 characters so you can still tell values apart.

I didn't find the exact name of the entropy detector, so look it up with `--list-kinds`.

## Alternative: cleansh (v0.1.11, Dec 2025, MIT/Apache-2.0)
cleansh covers the same ground. Pick it if you'd rather not install Rust, because it has prebuilt binaries on [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/KarmaYama/cleansh-workspace). You can also run `cargo install cleansh`.
```sh
docker logs my-container | cleansh sanitize
cat server.log | cleansh sanitize --engine entropy   # also catch unknown-format secrets
```
Extras over leakguard:
- It shortens `/home/<user>` paths to `~/`.
- It can copy the output to the clipboard (`-c`) or show a diff (`-d`).
- It accepts custom YAML rules through `--config`.

Some "team" features in it are inactive stubs, but the sanitizing itself is fully open source.

## Other options I found but didn't look into
- [hexredact](https://github.com/happygream/hexredact) replaces each value with a consistent token, so the same IP always becomes the same placeholder. That keeps logs traceable, which helps when you ask an AI to debug them.
- [local-redact](https://github.com/sumankrsh/local-redact) is a Python command-line tool that reads stdin and writes stdout.
- [rog7/redact](https://github.com/rog7/redact) is a simple Python script.
- Microsoft Presidio is well known but much heavier (Python plus an NLP model). It focuses on personal data more than API keys and is overkill for piping logs.

**Caveat:** all of these are best-effort pattern matchers, and leakguard's docs say so too. Secrets without a recognizable shape can still get through, such as a plain `password=hunter2` or an internal hostname. Turn on the entropy detector, add your own hostnames and names with `--redact-literal`, and skim the result before pasting.

Sources:
- [leakguard on docs.rs](https://docs.rs/crate/leakguard/latest/source/src/bin/leakguard.rs)
- [cleansh on docs.rs](https://docs.rs/cleansh/0.1.7/i686-unknown-linux-gnu/cleansh/)
- [hexredact](https://github.com/happygream/hexredact)
- [local-redact](https://github.com/sumankrsh/local-redact)
- [rog7/redact](https://github.com/rog7/redact)
